content:
Over fifteen years monitoring the public sector: what we've learned about government investment

More than 200,000 projects and USD 20 billion under supervision led us to an uncomfortable conclusion: the problem is rarely a lack of data; it is a lack of visibility into it.

[KPI] 200K::Projects monitored | $20B::Dollars under control | 15::Years in operation

The data exists; the visibility doesn't

When a public entity opens its systems to us for the first time, we almost never find an information gap. We find the opposite: spreadsheets, PDF meeting records, emails with attachments, inspection reports, SECOP records. The data is there. What's missing is the ability to look at it all together and reach a conclusion the same day.

That gap between having data and having visibility is where projects are lost. A delay a supervisor spots in the field takes weeks to reach the person who can decide to fix it. By then, the cost overrun has already occurred.

The problem with public oversight is not a lack of information. It's that information reaches decision-makers late and in fragments.

Three recurring patterns

1. Information lives in silos

Procurement has its data, finance has its own, and inspectors report through yet another channel. Nobody is lying; nobody sees the whole picture. Manual consolidation eats up the time that should go into analysis.

2. Reporting replaces oversight

Many entities confuse reporting with oversight. A monthly report creates a sense of vigilance, but a report describes the past. Real oversight requires alerts the moment a deviation occurs, not thirty days later.

3. Evidence can't be verified

A photo without a date, coordinates or an accountable person is not evidence; it's just an image. Traceability requires verifiable support for every reported milestone.

What changes with visibility

  • Decisions stop relying on intuition and start relying on the actual state of execution.
  • Disagreements between contractors and inspectors are settled with evidence, not competing accounts.
  • Senior management stops requesting reports and starts checking the dashboard directly.
  • Citizens can verify how their area's budget was spent.

What's next

The next frontier isn't better record-keeping; it's anticipation. With analytics and artificial intelligence, we can identify which projects are most likely to fall behind before the delay materializes. That is what we're working on at IK Labs today.
